title: Yen Gap Audit for Legacy Seven Owners
one_liner: A flat-fee LINE audit that takes HQ's own AI order proposal as the baseline and shows Kansai multi-store Seven-Eleven owners, per item and delivery slot, the yen gap between what HQ suggests and what their own 15/85 contract says they should order.
customer: Owner-operators (individuals or small corporations) running 3 to 10 legacy-contract Seven-Eleven stores in Osaka, Kyoto and Hyogo, who have a contract renewal or a new-store offer within 24 months. Legacy stores are the narrow wedge because Seven's new contract (50/50 disposal share, effective autumn 2027) applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned, so the 15/85 asymmetry persists on existing stores for years. Multi-store owners are the segment that can pay (a 5-store owner pays about 34k yen a month against roughly 4.7M yen of food discarded per store per year), that is most exposed to OFC pressure, and that faces the legacy-versus-new-contract expansion decision. One chain means one contract model. Lawson and FamilyMart wait until their subsidy formulas are verified.
problem: HQ's AI proposes a quantity but never says whose payoff it maximizes. With an 85% owner share of disposal loss, the owner's critical ratio is about 22% (keeps about 24 yen per rice ball sold, loses about 85 yen per one binned) while HQ's is about 70% (earns about 36, loses about 15). Owners cannot audit the proposal and fear the OFC if they deviate. Judges flagged three weaknesses: the asymmetry fades on post-2027 contracts, HQ's markdown push since May 2024 (about 300 items, alerts about 2 hours before expiry) commoditizes a markdown clock, and willingness to pay for software is unproven. Earlier framing as a competing ordering AI also invites a fight with three chains' in-house AI.
solution: Not a better forecaster, a payoff transform. If HQ's recommended quantity approximates the 70th percentile of demand and the owner's optimum is the 22nd, the owner's cut is about 1.3 standard deviations of the slot's demand spread (about 3.9 units for an item averaging 10 with a spread of 3). The tool therefore needs only the HQ proposal (photo of the order terminal screen or printout), the order actually placed, and the store's hourly sales history to estimate the spread. It returns (1) a ranked Yen Gap sheet: the ten biggest expected-yen differences per delivery slot between HQ's proposal and the owner-optimal quantity under that store's own royalty tier and disposal share; (2) an audit of HQ's markdown clock: for the roughly 300 alerted items and for non-alerted items, whether 'two hours before expiry' is earlier or later than the owner-optimal sticker time given the store's sell-through curve; (3) a neutral 'why I ordered differently' one-pager citing expected value under the owner's contract, shown to the OFC only if the owner chooses; (4) a monthly portfolio page with each store's critical ratio and true hourly wage after royalty and own labor, plus an annual memo on whether the next store should be a legacy expansion or a new-contract store. Nothing touches HQ systems.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises 54 yen to 1,231 yen on 1 Oct 2026 and Diamond reported a Seven internal simulation with franchisee profit falling to about one third if wages rise on flat sales. HQ AI ordering is now default at all three chains, so owners follow suggestions they cannot audit. Seven's June 2026 announcement of a new contract with a 50% disposal share concedes the point, and creates a two-tier portfolio (legacy versus new stores) that owners have never had to model. Photo OCR of Japanese printouts and cheap LLM-based structuring make a per-owner concierge audit affordable in 2026, which was not true in 2019.
revenue_model: Entry offer: a paid 30,000 yen '30-day Yen Gap Audit' on one store (credited toward the first 3 months), which tests willingness to pay before any subscription. Then a flat 6,800 yen per store per month (bundle discount at 5+ stores). An annual 150,000 yen next-store-or-renewal decision memo, timed to the moment an owner holds a real 10M-yen decision. Optional 15% gain-share only where a signed baseline exists, so revenue does not depend on disputed savings. Ex-OFC consultants and accountants who refer owners get a 20% revenue share. Bottom-up, if about 5,000 legacy stores sit with 3+ store owners in this segment (an assumption to verify), that is roughly 400M yen a year at full penetration.
non_obvious_insight: The forecast is not the scarce thing, the payoff is. HQ's proposal already encodes a demand distribution, so an owner-side tool can back out the implied quantile and shift it, needing only a spread estimate from the owner's own sales sheets. That makes the product tiny to build and easy to back-test on the founder's three stores. It also flips the political framing: the owner is not overriding HQ's AI, he is applying his own contract to its numbers. Counter-positioning is real, since HQ cannot ship a screen that says its AI is tuned to the wrong payoff without conceding the conflict the JFTC and METI panel already scrutinize.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: back-test on the founder's three stores, comparing HQ proposals against realized sales and disposals, estimating the implied quantile and spread per category, and computing the yen gap. Day 3: one-hour paid review by a franchise lawyer of the confidentiality and third-party data clauses. Days 8-20: sell 10 paid 30,000-yen audits through 3-5 ex-OFC consultants, one or two accountants serving multi-store owners, and Kansai owner LINE and Facebook groups. Kill or pivot signal: fewer than 3 paid at 30,000 yen. Days 21-30: deliver audits, convert the willing to 6,800 yen flat with a 60-day money-back guarantee, and publish a one-page legacy-versus-new-contract critical-ratio table (22% versus about 36%) as owner-to-owner content.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. The unserved wedge is: HQ says X, your own contract math says Y, the yen difference is Z, plus contract-aware multi-store economics. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified. | How this version avoids them: Seven, Lawson and FamilyMart AI ordering and Seven's markdown push are treated as the baseline input, not a rival. The product does not compete on forecast accuracy and audits HQ's markdown clock instead of inventing another. Sinops/Sato and Wasteless/Afresh/Shelf Engine sell to retailers and inherit the retailer's payoff, and none uses a franchisee's contract terms. Too Good To Go is an outlet for surplus, not a decision tool. The Okayama union and ex-OFC consultants give advice without calculators, so they become referral partners rather than substitutes, and the channel does not depend on the small Okayama union. Narrowing to legacy Seven stores avoids the per-chain contract complexity and the shrinking-asymmetry problem of post-2027 new stores.

title: Solar Job Escrow: Bankruptcy-Proof Project Records
one_liner: A neutral escrow that captures every financed solar job's permit, design, serial and step-in authorizations before the installer fails. The installer pays per job, the lender enforces deposits through milestone funding, and cure is paid from the final milestone the lender is still holding.
customer: Payer: mid-size residential installers (300-3,000 loan-financed jobs a year) that need financing access and a trust signal after Freedom Forever. Gatekeeper and co-seller: dealer-risk and credit heads at solar lenders and credit unions (GoodLeap, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human-type), who can make escrow a dealer-tier condition. Channel: installer CRM, design and project-management platforms that embed the deposit.
problem: When an installer dies, the permits, interconnection applications, PE-stamped designs, serials and portal logins are locked in the dead company's name, and the lender starts from zero. Every other party (lender, homeowner, trustee) finds out after the fact. Before failure, all of that data exists and is easy to copy. After failure it is expensive to reconstruct. The parent product only starts once the loss has occurred, which is why it is lumpy, price-pressured and crowded.
solution: Each job auto-deposits a continuity pack at each milestone: signed contract, permit application and approval, PE-stamped design set, interconnection application number, equipment serials by BOM, and time-stamped site photos. Two pre-signed documents go with it. The homeowner signs a successor-contractor authorization as an addendum at the point of sale, and the installer signs a step-in consent. A written trigger (insolvency, license suspension, or 60 days of no activity) releases the pack to a designated successor. The lender's funding portal requires a complete pack before releasing M1 or M2, so deposits cannot be skipped. Trigger jobs are cured at a pre-agreed per-AHJ rate card. The cure is paid from the last milestone (M3) the lender still holds on that job, plus a small installer holdback. Lenders also get a continuity score per dealer (record completeness, PTO lag, license and lien status). Homeowners get a 'job protected' certificate that installers can use in sales.
why_now: Freedom Forever's collapse made 'will you still be here at PTO?' the first objection at every kitchen table, and made lenders' dealer-risk teams look for controls beyond credit checks. The 25D end is shrinking installer margins and raising failure odds. Agentic capture and CRM APIs make per-job record collection cheap enough for a $60-100 fee. ABS investors can now cite a specific 2026 case when they ask sponsors about continuity.
revenue_model: Installer pays $60-100 per job (about 0.2-0.3% of a $30-35k job). Lender pays a platform fee of $5-10k a month for dealer continuity scoring and pack access. On a trigger, cure work is billed at $1.5-4k per job plus a $500 PTO bonus, funded from the held M3 milestone. Later: a workmanship warranty backed by the reserve, and a recognized 'backup installer' role in ABS structures. Illustration: 3 pilot installers at 800 jobs each is roughly $145-240k a year in deposit fees before lender fees or cure revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The cure budget already exists. On many dealer-channel loans the final milestone (roughly 10-25% of the loan) is not paid until PTO, so on every stranded job the lender is still holding thousands of dollars that would have gone to the dead installer. The only missing piece is a pre-signed right to spend it. And the escrow has an enforcement mechanism that software-escrow lacked: the lender controls the money, so 'no pack, no milestone payment' means installers deposit because that is how they get paid. The party who needs the protection (the lender) is not the party who pays (the installer), and making escrow a sales badge and a dealer-tier perk closes that gap.
first_30_days: Draft the continuity pack spec and the successor-contractor authorization with a solar or construction attorney. Map contractor-of-record change rules for the 10 largest AHJs and top 2-3 utilities in one metro. Recruit 5 installers through former installer ops people and offer a free 90-day pilot in exchange for the badge. Call 3 lender dealer-risk heads with a one-page pitch: escrowed dealers get faster funding or lower holdbacks, and you get a first-call cure vendor. Target 3 installer LOIs and 1 lender pilot letter by day 30, and first live deposits by day 60. Riskiest assumption to test: will a lender change its funding conditions for a pilot dealer group. Test it with a credit union first.
lineage: mutation of I1175 ('Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GreenLancer (Solar Repair / O&M network), Lender in-house step-in (GoodLeap, Sunrun, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human, Participate, Project Solar; also Dividend Finance), Atma Energy (installer taking over stranded Freedom Forever jobs), Local rescue and completion contractors (Revival Solar, ECG Solar, Optimus Energy Solutions, Advance Solar, Solar Discovery). White space: The unserved wedge is portfolio-level, event-driven triage, not crews. (1) Forensic records recovery at scale. No competitor found sells a forensic pack per stranded loan (AHJ permit file, utility interconnection record, dead installer's CRM and design files, distributor and consignment serials, photo audit) sorted into cure tiers with a cost-to-cure and expected-PTO dashboard across a lender's whole book. GreenLancer and the local rescue firms all work job by job. (2) Servicers, credit unions and ABS trustees without operations. The seven Freedom Forever financiers have ops teams, and Sunrun and GoodLeap have crews. Solar Servicing LLC (which took over Mosaic's servicing), credit unions, bank holders and ABS investors have no step-in playbook. I found no completion vendor aimed at them. (3) Legacy stranded books. Titan (an estimated 150,000 households), SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, Mosaic-financed loans and others. Lenders may not know which loans sit on de-energized systems, so an identify-then-cure offer has little competition. (4) Standby retainer plus pre-negotiated per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer playbooks for the next failure. Not white space: the first-wave Freedom Forever completion work. The stay-relief order dates to about August 2026, so the seven named financiers have probably already picked contractors, and GreenLancer says it already serves seven financiers. | How this version avoids them: GreenLancer, local rescue contractors and Atma all start after failure, job by job, for an already-staffed lender. This owns the pre-failure moment, sits inside the dealer agreement and the installer's workflow, and earns recurring per-job revenue from installers. When a trigger fires, the company is first-called under a pre-signed rate card and can subcontract to GreenLancer-style shops or local firms. Lender in-house step-in desks have no installer-side records capture, and installers work with 3-5 lenders and will not deposit into five separate lender portals, so neutral multi-lender escrow wins. Solar Insure and OhmSnap serve owners after bankruptcy, and Enphase's program is post-PTO. Main risk is a big lender building a proprietary version, which the neutral multi-lender position is meant to counter.

title: Canary Humans: Leak-Testing ID Verification Vendors
one_liner: Put consenting, instrumented real people through a platform's ID and age checks, then prove whether the vendor kept, leaked or resold their documents.
customer: Trust-and-safety, privacy and vendor-risk leads at platforms that outsource ID or age checks (dating apps, gig and rental marketplaces, cannabis and vape retail tech, crypto exchanges, adult and gaming operators), and the cyber insurers underwriting them.
problem: Platforms pick verification vendors on a SOC 2 badge and a promise to delete images quickly, and customers cannot test that promise. AU10TIX, Discord's support vendor, Persona and IDScan were all breached in 2024-26. IDScan reported 150M+ licence scans stolen in Sept 2026. Ofcom and state AGs judge platforms on 'reasonable steps', so the platform owns its vendor's failure.
solution: Recruit a few hundred paid 'canary humans' with unique emails, phones, addresses and ID numbers, and enrol them in the customer's live verification flow with the customer's consent. Then run scheduled tests: deletion requests, access requests to the vendor and its sub-processors, and monitoring of breach dumps, data-broker files, phishing and spam lists and dark-market listings for canary-unique strings. The deliverable is a quarterly retention and leakage attestation with evidence, usable in vendor contracts, cyber-insurance applications and regulator files. It also produces a public 'retention half-life' benchmark by vendor.
why_now: IDScan's Sept 2026 breach (150M+ licences) and the Persona, AU10TIX and Discord-vendor incidents showed that certified vendors leak. The EU's 31 Dec 2026 age-verification rollout deadline will push thousands more sites to outsource checks. Ofcom has opened 90+ investigations and issued fines. The Delve scandal (Mar-Apr 2026) showed that paper compliance is not proof.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per platform per vendor tested, an insurer portfolio programme (per-insured fee), and a breach-forensics retainer. Later add an efficacy-proof product for privacy-removal services.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance automation (Vanta is at roughly $300M ARR) certifies that controls exist on paper, and nobody tests outcomes. A verifier's product is a promise to forget, and the only way to audit a promise about data is to plant traceable data and watch where it surfaces. Security calls these honeytokens and direct marketers call them seed lists, but nobody has applied the trick to verification vendors.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 privacy-minded volunteers at $100-200 each with signed consent and a legal review (no fake IDs, real people only). Pitch three mid-size dating, gig or cannabis-tech platforms and one cyber MGA. Offer a free 90-day pilot against one vendor under NDA. Publish an anonymised benchmark from the pilot to generate inbound.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Vanta (compliance automation), SecurityScorecard, Transcend (privacy/DSR orchestration), Age Check Certification Scheme (ACCS) and Age Verification Providers Association (AVPA) standards ecosystem. White space: Research limits first. WebSearch hit its 200-call session cap before I could run any of the planned startup, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt searches, so I did not verify the absence of a direct startup. I used WebFetch on named pages and GitHub repo searches instead. Wikipedia and vendor-site fetches turned up no company that recruits real, consenting individuals, enrols them in a platform's live ID or age-check flow, files deletion and access requests with the vendor and its sub-processors, watches for the canary strings, and issues an attestation. GitHub searches for open-source tools returned nothing relevant.

What is unserved: outcome-based, adversarial proof of the promise to forget. Incumbents cover the adjacent layers.
- Compliance automation (Vanta) covers whether controls exist on paper.
- Standards bodies (ACCS, Kantara, AVPA/ISO 27566) cover process and control audits.
- SecurityScorecard covers passive outside-in ratings.
- DSR orchestration (Transcend) covers a customer's own deletions.
- Honeytoken vendors cover a customer's own intrusions.
- HIBP-style monitors cover leaked-string detection.

The specific unserved piece is an independent, real-human, live-flow test with a public per-vendor retention benchmark.

Structural weaknesses of the pitch:
- Real government ID numbers cannot be unique canaries. Only emails, phones, addresses and name variants are. Leak detection depends on those fields surfacing in dumps, and image-only dumps are hard to search.
- The base rate of any given vendor leaking in a quarter is low. Most attestations would say nothing found, which is weak evidence. Retention and deletion behaviour, tested through DSARs and access requests, is the part canaries can actually prove.
- Vendors may treat the enrolments as terms-of-service violations. Customer consent helps but does not remove that risk.
- Privacy-preserving designs such as on-device age estimation and reusable digital ID could shrink the retention problem that this idea audits.

title: Camp-Road Closing Rescue Plus Resale Toll
one_liner: A Maine-only, attorney-supervised service that runs the statutory neighbor meeting, records an enforceable assessment-lien covenant, and then issues a paid road-status letter on every future sale on that road.
customer: Wedge: closing attorneys and title agents handling lake-camp, second-home and rural sales in Maine's lakes region and midcoast (start with the 5 to 8 firms that do the most camp closings). The payer at the table is the seller, or the buyer via negotiated credit. Out-of-state second-home buyers and their lenders are the ones who insist on a maintenance agreement. Listing agents are a secondary channel in the Oct-Feb off-season, when they prep camps for spring listing.
problem: Maine Title 23 section 3101 (text re-checked today) lets as few as 3 parcels petition a notary to call a meeting, lets a majority vote set assessments, and shields board members from civil liability. It contains no lien or collection remedy. The parent research counted 4 parcels, but the fetched text says 3 parcels held by 3 different owners. So the statute is a vote without teeth, and nobody runs the vote. No closing attorney will chase 14 owners for proxies at a flat closing fee, so the sale stalls or closes on a handshake. The parent's own flaws sit on top of this. Its $12-25 per household per month is 6 to 12 times PayHOA's price anchor. Holding dues float triggers trust-account rules. A 5-8% procurement fee is a conflict of interest. Its plan to have attorneys send deals for a flat fee is a RESPA Section 8 trap, because 12 CFR 1024.14 bars referral fees and unearned fees in federally related mortgage transactions and permits payment only for services actually performed.
solution: Sell 'Meeting-in-a-Box' as a fixed-scope, attorney-supervised package. We do the non-billable grunt work: map benefiting parcels from the registry of deeds and county GIS, serve statutory notice, run the notary-called meeting (in person plus absentee and proxy ballots), keep minutes, collect the officer slate and a treasurer, take a baseline road-condition photo log, and handle recording. The supervising attorney, either the closing attorney or our contracted Maine counsel, owns the legal instrument: a recorded covenant that adds what the statute lacks (assessment lien running with the land, successor obligation, reserve requirement, estoppel-letter mechanism). We build no dues software and hold no money. Each association opens a bank account with a treasurer, and we hand over a checklist plus a PayHOA or plain-ACH setup guide. After formation we run one annual notice-and-meeting cycle and issue a road-status letter (dues current, no open assessments, maintenance agreement on record) whenever a house on the road sells. This works like the HOA resale certificate. No referral fees are paid to anyone. Attorneys bill their own legal work, and our fee is a disclosed third-party service line.
why_now: Maine's statute already exists, so formation is process work rather than a legal breakthrough. Post-2020 in-migration put many out-of-state buyers on camp roads they do not understand. Housing turnover is historically low (roughly 3-4% a year, an assumption to confirm), so every stalled closing costs a seller and an agent real money. Hurricane Helene's NC private-road program showed that aid and repair money flow only to an organized counterparty with a named contact, which makes 'pre-formed association' a sellable feature. Oct-Feb is slack season for Maine camp closings, so attorneys have time to try a new workflow before spring listings. Cheap document automation and e-signature make proxy and absentee ballot logistics a small cost rather than a paralegal week.
revenue_model: Formation: $1,400 flat per road, paid at closing from seller proceeds or by the neighborhood, disclosed as a third-party service. Attorney legal review is billed separately by the attorney at roughly $300-500. Recurring: $200 per association per year, flat rather than per household, for annual notice, meeting, officer changes and records. Transaction toll: $175 per road-status letter, paid by the seller at each future sale. With about 9 coordinator hours plus recording fees per formation, gross margin should be near 60-65%. Rough year-1 target is 40 roads, or about $56k formation plus $8k recurring. At 300 roads with about 18 homes each and 3-4% turnover, resale letters add about $35k a year. That makes a real but modest Maine business, and the scalable asset is the state-by-state playbook plus the registry.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in Maine is not the entity, since the statute lets neighbors make one, and not the legal template, which is a commodity. It is the person who runs the meeting and the recorded covenant that gives assessments teeth. The first closing buys the association, and every later closing pays a toll, so a formed road becomes a perpetual, transaction-priced revenue stream. That toll avoids the PayHOA per-household price anchor and sits where the money is, in seller proceeds. Because the attorney does the legal work under supervision and is never paid to refer, the attorney channel is RESPA-clean and the attorney stops being the substitute. Over time title agents learn to ask for our letter, which creates switching costs because the association's officer and records live with us.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain a Maine real estate attorney on a flat $3-5k engagement to draft the covenant with lien language, the estoppel-letter form and the meeting script. Have that attorney confirm the lien is enforceable when drafted as a recorded covenant and confirm the RESPA-safe fee structure. Weeks 1-3: hold 20 calls with lakes-region and midcoast closing attorneys and title agents and ask which of their last 12 months' closings hit a road issue, what happened, and what they would pay to have it handled. Weeks 2-4: run 2 pilot roads (one tied to a live or stalled closing) at a $600 pilot price, and measure owner participation rate, days to majority vote, and hours per road. By day 30, get 3 firms to sign a one-page agreement to route their next road problem to us at $1,400. The riskiest assumption to kill early is whether attorneys will buy outsourced meeting logistics rather than absorb it.
lineage: mutation of I0048 ('Private Road Associations in a Box'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:
- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest. | How this version avoids them: PayHOA: we build no dues product and do not compete at about $2 per household. We price per association and per sale, and PayHOA is a setup option we recommend, so it is a partner rather than a rival. Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC: they serve incorporated associations with managers, whereas we create the legal counterparty they cannot. DIY templates and local attorneys (Nolo, LegalZoom-style forms): a template gives no notice, vote, proxy, minutes or recording service, and the attorney is our channel and supervising counsel rather than a substitute, because we take the work they cannot bill profitably. Maine statute: we productize it and plug its missing lien with the recorded covenant. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: a demand signal, and our 'pre-formed association with a named contact' is exactly what such programs require. Local road-association managers and bookkeepers (unidentified): they sell ongoing bookkeeping, not closing-triggered formation, and could be subcontractors for annual administration.

title: Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records
one_liner: Turn public US import records into supplier-owned reputation credentials and audit-ready reasonable-care dossiers that prove a factory is a real manufacturer.
customer: Small and mid-size US importers of record (Amazon and Shopify brands, furniture, hardware and apparel distributors) re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey. Customs brokers are a channel, and factories are the second payer.
problem: The importer of record is investigated first, and liability turns on whether it exercised reasonable care about the supplier's origin claims. In August 2026 the White House published a report on transshipment, a 40% penalty tariff applies, and CBP has expanded inspections of shipments from Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Mexico. Small importers cannot tell a real factory from a trading company or a re-labeller, and sourcing agents' claims are unverifiable.
solution: Supplier Proof. Build a profile per factory from three or more years of US import records (shipper and consignee names, volumes, product codes, ports, cadence) plus corporate registry and location data, flag anomalies such as volume beyond plausible capacity, mismatched product codes or shell-company addresses, and add optional local inspector visits. Factories claim and verify their profile and can consent to name repeat buyers as references. The output is a dossier the importer can hand to a broker or to CBP.
why_now: Tariff enforcement moved in 2025-26 from headline rates to origin verification, and the August 2026 transshipment report has put importer liability on every compliance officer's desk. Sourcing shifts away from China are happening now, so millions of dollars of orders are going to unfamiliar factories.
revenue_model: Importer subscriptions of $149-499 per month, $150-400 per dossier, inspector visits passed through at a margin, and $600-1,200 per year from factories for a verified credential once importers demand it.
non_obvious_insight: Import records are the only unforgeable cross-border reputation ledger for factories, but they are sold as raw rows to analysts. Repackaged as supplier-owned credentials with a reasonable-care wrapper, a data product becomes a compliance product with a real budget line: avoiding a 40% penalty.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories (for example furniture and hardware from Vietnam and India). Auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles and hand-audit 20. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers. Sell the first 10 dossiers at $250 each and use them to refine the scoring.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ImportGenius, Panjiva (S&P Global Market Intelligence), Descartes Datamyne, ImportYeti. White space: The narrow wedge that appears unserved is a fixed-price, human-reviewed 'reasonable-care file' for a small US importer, sold through customs brokers. The SMB importer (Amazon or Shopify brand, or a $2-50M distributor) needs one factory checked before one PO. Enterprise tools (Sayari, Altana, Tradeverifyd, Trademo, Exiger) are sold by demo and are priced and scoped for large compliance teams. Data tools (ImportGenius, Panjiva, Datamyne, ImportYeti) sell rows and leave interpretation to the analyst. Inspectors (QIMA) and sourcing agents (Sourcify) sell physical checks, not a documentary file that maps to CBP's reasonable-care standard. The part I found nobody offering is a factory-claimed profile with consent-based buyer references, which is a two-sided credential. No visible player runs a supplier-owned reputation credential built on customs ledgers. However, the wedge is thin. (1) ImportGenius already markets 'supplier verification via shipping history' at the same $229-449/mo price band. (2) The raw-data floor is free or near-free. (3) Any one of Altana, Trademo or ImportGenius could add a 'transshipment risk report' feature quickly. (4) The factory-pays credential side has no demonstrated demand and needs a two-sided marketplace. Risks I could not check with the exhausted search budget: whether resale of licensed bill-of-lading data is allowed, that US import records often name the forwarder or trading company as shipper instead of the factory, that importers can request confidentiality under 19 CFR 103.31, and that no CBP safe-harbor exists for third-party dossiers.

title: Auto Loan-End Event Exchange for Add-On Refunds
one_liner: Start by recovering unearned add-on refunds on repossessed and charged-off loans for small lenders on pure contingency (cash the lender itself keeps), then turn those lender-attested loan-end events into a neutral exchange that administrators, carriers and regulators plug into, so refunds become a statutory event pushed to the administrator instead of a claim the borrower must pull.
customer: Stage 1: collections and recovery managers at credit unions and community banks with $200M to $3B in auto loans (too small for in-house recovery teams), plus the collection agencies and recovery BPOs that serve them. Stage 2 payers: GAP and service-contract administrators and their fronting or contractual-liability carriers and reinsurers; regulators get free access. Governance: founding lenders receive equity or rebates through a cooperative structure such as a CUSO.
problem: At repossession or charge-off, the unearned refund on financed GAP, service contracts and other add-ons is collectible cash for the lender and shrinks the deficiency billed to the member. Small lenders rarely chase it because each administrator has its own paper process and the dealer chargeback fight breeds stalling. The deeper failure is informational: where a state requires automatic refunds on payoff (the parent cites New Jersey; verify), the administrator cannot comply because nobody tells it the loan ended. No one sits between the lender who knows and the administrator who owes, so every refund is a bilateral fight with no shared standard, no SLA and no scoreboard.
solution: Stage 1, sellable within 6 months, is a Repo Refund Desk. The lender drops a monthly file of repossessions and charge-offs plus contract images (secure upload, no core integration). The system reads the add-ons, matches administrators, computes refunds by state rule, files cancellations under the lender's assignment of unearned premiums, and tracks to payment. Refunds post to the lender's loan account, cutting both the write-off and the member's deficiency. Fee: 20 to 25% of cash actually recovered, nothing upfront. Stage 2: every processed case becomes a signed loan-end event (VIN, contract ID, event type, date, products, computed refund). Publish an open Loan-End Event schema and API; administrators get structured, lender-attested cancellation requests in their own intake format, cheaper than manual intake and a defensible statutory trigger. Payoff and total-loss events join (the parent's payoff-desk plug-in becomes a free module). Stage 3: carriers and reinsurers get true early-termination curves and refund-SLA dashboards; regulators get a free supervisory view; later a settlement layer and a refund-advance facility.
why_now: Record subprime delinquency and roughly 3M repossessions a year create a large event flow today. 84-month loans mean add-ons are unearned at almost every repossession. LLM contract reading cuts per-case processing from tens of dollars to cents, which is what makes contingency pricing work. State regulators and private plaintiffs are filling a federal enforcement retreat (verify), raising the value of an audit trail. Core-processor API marketplaces and CUSOs make plug-in distribution to credit unions cheaper than a direct sales force (verify).
revenue_model: Stage 1: 20 to 25% contingency on recovered cash. Illustration to validate in the free retrospective audit: a lender with $1B in auto loans, about 1,000 repossessions a year, 45% with financed add-ons, about $700 average unearned, 60% currently unclaimed is roughly $190K of new cash a year and a $40K to $47K annual fee. Stage 2: administrators pay $2 to $5 per attested event plus a compliance subscription; carriers and reinsurers pay $50K to $250K a year for termination and SLA data; regulators free. Stage 3: a 0.5 to 1% network fee on refunds settled through the exchange, and a refund-advance facility funded with outside capital. Stage 1 alone is a viable small business; the exchange is the venture-scale option.
non_obvious_insight: The stalling problem is less about willingness than information: nobody tells the administrator the loan ended, and the one party that knows, the lender, has never had a reason to say so. Refund-on-repossession, unlike refund-on-payoff, is the lender's own cash, so the lender pays willingly, and the same act produces the signed events that convert each administrator's private float into a scoreboarded, regulator-visible liability. The exchange's real asset is the true early-termination rate for financed add-ons, which no administrator, reinsurer or regulator can observe today because they see only claimed cancellations, not loans that actually ended. That number prices and reserves every GAP and service-contract program.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2: build administrator playbooks for the 20 largest administrators and 10 states (as in the parent) and the pro-rata engine. Weeks 1 to 3: offer 5 credit unions or community banks a free retrospective audit of their last 12 months of repossessions and charge-offs and report the cash left on the table. Weeks 3 to 4: sign 2 on 25% contingency and process live cases weekly; recruit one collection agency or recovery BPO as a reseller. In parallel, publish Loan-End Event schema v0.1 openly, and send an SLA-scoreboard mockup built from the first 100 cases to compliance heads at 10 administrators and consumer-services staff at 2 state insurance departments. Target: $25K of recovered cash logged, 3 lender LOIs, 1 administrator willing to receive structured requests.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Origence (formerly CU Direct) - loan origination/indirect platform (CUDL), Assurant (F&I administrator and TPA), Unverified: consumer GAP/VSC refund-claim services (contingency), Unverified: in-house lender recovery and collections teams and BPO vendors. 1. I found no direct competitor selling a payoff-triggered GAP/VSC refund plug-in to credit unions. Origence, the dominant CU indirect-lending platform, and Assurant, a major administrator, show no such product on their homepages.

2. Genuinely unserved and specific, if the market read holds:
   - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.
   - A 50-state pro-rata rules engine combined with an administrator-by-administrator cancellation-requirements database.
   - An attorney-ready audit of repossession deficiency notices that reconciles unearned add-on credits. Consumer-bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid are plausible buyers, because the lender's or dealer's incentive runs against the borrower.

   - The claim that the lender never owned the product is shaky. Under many state retail installment sales acts, and under the FTC Holder Rule, the assignee or holder can carry refund and credit obligations.    - A 20-30% success fee taken from a member's own refund has poor fee optics for a credit union. It also conflicts with the idea's own member-experience rationale.
   - On payoff, the refund goes to the borrower, so the CU gets no direct economic benefit. The CU's incentive is goodwill and compliance, not revenue.
   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. | How this version avoids them: Origence and other LOS vendors are lender-only tools that can bolt on a lender feature but not a neutral two-sided exchange that administrators trust; treat them as distribution partners and open the schema so it becomes their integration target rather than a fight. Assurant-type administrators are the counterparty in stage 1 but customers in stage 2, because a lender-attested event is safer for them than a disputed consumer request; dealer-owned reinsurers that profit from stale reserves are the natural losers and would not build this. Consumer refund sites are sidestepped: no consumer acquisition, no SEO. The direct-overlap risk, in-house lender recovery teams and BPOs, exists mostly at large lenders (per unverified research), so start with the long tail of credit unions and community banks that have none and sell through their agencies. A cross-lender event dataset cannot be built by any single in-house team.

title: Appraisal Workfile Trustee for Retired and Deceased Appraisers
one_liner: A neutral custodian that holds a retiring or deceased appraiser's workfiles for 10 years, proves they were never altered, and answers subpoenas, board letters and lender QC requests so the retiree or widow never has to.
customer: Wedge: sole-proprietor certified residential appraisers aged 62+ who have just gone inactive or announced retirement in 3-4 states (TX, OH, PA, CO), plus heirs and executors of appraisers who die or become incapacitated. These people usually already hold a free LIA or OREP retirement tail, so the money risk is covered and the missing piece is the defense file. Scale payers: E&O administrators and state appraiser associations (loss-control benefit). Requesters (attorneys, lenders, boards) pay production fees where rules allow.
problem: USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (or 2 years after a judicial proceeding ends), and regulators can act later. A retiree's copy sits on an aging laptop, a USB drive or a software subscription that lapses. The free tail pays defense costs but does not preserve or produce the file, and a workfile with no independent proof of when it was finalized is easy to attack as backfilled. When an appraiser dies, board letters and subpoenas land on a widow with no idea what a workfile is. Nobody answers a subpoena on the retiree's behalf: software vendors store files, they do not act as agent.
solution: Product v1, 'Seal and Hold': (1) A 60-minute import from a la mode, ClickFORMS or ACI exports or a drive image. Every file is hashed and stamped with a third-party RFC 3161 timestamp, kept in write-once encrypted storage with an index by date, client and address. (2) A custodian agreement naming the Trustee as records custodian and agent for production, plus a notice letter to the state board. (3) A production desk that handles subpoenas, board requests, lender QC and repurchase requests and E&O carrier requests, notifies the retiree or estate, and bills the requester. (4) An estate trigger: named heirs, a death or incapacity switch and pre-filled paperwork. (5) Retention beyond the minimum, with legal-hold extension. Deliberately excluded: trainees, client transfer, earn-outs, tail brokerage.
why_now: UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. WorkingRE's 2026 survey says 31% plan to leave within 3 years and 57% are over 60, so a predictable wave of exits is starting. Free LIA and OREP tails have made the money side a solved problem, which leaves the file as the remaining exposure. Immutable cold storage and third-party timestamping are commodity-cheap, so intake per retiree is under an hour of ops time.
revenue_model: $695 one-time for 10-year custody including 3 productions (or $19/month). $995 estate or heir rush plan. Extra productions at $195-450, requester-pays where state rules permit, otherwise billed to the retiree or estate. Group license to E&O administrators and associations at roughly $8-15 per insured per year as loss control (needs validation). Cold storage for about 100 GB costs around $1 per month, so gross margin is 85%+ and the real cost is the production desk and counsel. A two-person team breaks even around 500 custodies a year (assumption).
non_obvious_insight: The free tail pays the lawyer, but a claim is won or lost on whether the appraiser can produce a file that provably existed in that form on that date. A retiree's own drive cannot prove non-alteration, while a neutral custodian with hash chains and third-party timestamps can. So this is closer to a notary or escrow than to storage, which is why software vendors paid by the user cannot credibly sell it and why insurers, estates and boards have reasons to care. Once the custodian is named in the retiree's board and carrier paperwork, moving away means new attestations, which creates switching costs.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain counsel for the custodian agreement and a state-by-state memo on retention, board notification, subpoena handling, and confirmation that we are not acting as an appraiser or AMC and no fee-splitting rule applies. Pull public rosters for TX, OH, PA and CO and flag licenses that went inactive or expired in the last 24 months and active licensees licensed 25+ years. Week 2: call 20 of them and pre-sell at $695 with a refund guarantee, then concierge-deliver the first 5 by hand (import 5 years of workfiles, timestamp, issue a custody certificate). Kill rule: fewer than 6 of 20 pay means pivot to insurer-funded only. Week 3: ask LIA and OREP claims managers, two independent E&O agents and one state appraiser association how workfile requests reach them today and whether they would co-brand or fund it as loss control. Meet 3 estate-planning attorneys. Week 4: run a 'What happens to your files when you retire' session through Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser forums and target 15 paid custodies.
lineage: mutation of I1039 ('Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors. | How this version avoids them: LIA and OREP sell tail money, not file preservation or production, so they are complements and a possible channel rather than rivals. a la mode/Cotality, ACI and ClickFORMS store files for a paying user but do not act as agent of record, sign attestations or answer subpoenas, and a vendor would take on legal exposure for a lapsed customer, so it is unlikely to respond soon. Aloft, Valligent, Solidifi, AXIS and PAREA are all trainee and supervisor plays, and this idea leaves that lane completely, which also removes the supervisor-of-record burden and trainee-count limits. AppraiseItNow buys only non-residential and specialty practices and offers no custody. Reggora and the AMC consolidators (Class Valuation, Atlas VMS) target lenders and AMC capacity, not individual retirees. Dropping earn-outs, percentage-of-trainee-fees and client transfer removes the fee-splitting, minimum-legal and weak-transferability flaws the research flagged.

title: Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return
one_liner: A per-return concierge that unwinds a cancelled used-car deal (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales tax, commissions) inside California's new 48-hour refund deadline. It then turns the return data into a return-risk pool.
customer: California used-car dealers, especially independents and BHPH lots that sell 30 to 200 used cars a month and have no back-office bench. They pay $195 to $250 per return, or a standby retainer. Later, insurers and MGAs buy the underwriting data.
problem: From Oct 1, 2026, SB 766 gives buyers a 3-day right to cancel a used vehicle priced at $50,000 or less. Within 48 hours of cancellation the dealer must cancel the contract and refund the buyer, less only the deductions the law allows for mileage and damage. That is easy to write and very hard to do. The cost of an unwind is the cascade, not the car. The dealer has to reach the lender that has funded or is holding the contract, cancel each service contract and GAP with its administrator, and charge back the F&I commission. It also has to reverse the title, registration and sales tax, refund the down payment and any trade, and document the vehicle condition to justify any deduction. Independents have never done this at volume, and one botched unwind creates a refund violation and a private-plaintiff claim.
solution: Unwind-as-a-service. The dealer forwards the cancellation notice. The desk runs a checklist workflow that notifies the lender, submits cancellations to administrators with the correct pro-rata or full-refund basis, prepares the DMV and tax reversals, calculates the refund and permitted deductions, and produces a compliance file that meets the two-year retention rule. A delivery-day photo and video capture link is bundled, because permitted deductions depend on condition documentation. After 6 months of volume, the desk holds the only dataset on return rates, timing and loss per return in a mandatory-return regime. That data is enough to price a per-unit return-risk cover (roughly $60 to $120 per used unit) through a licensed MGA or insurer partner.
why_now: The law takes effect Oct 1, 2026, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has had a mandatory 3-day return on used cars at this scale. The 2025 to 2026 run of subprime stress, roughly 30% of trade-ins underwater and repossessions at about 3M a year, means many buyers will discover mid-week that they can't afford the payment. That is the buyer most likely to use the cancellation right.
revenue_model: Flat fee per processed return ($195 to $250). Standby retainer of about $99 per month per store for priority handling. Phase 2: 10 to 20% of premium as an MGA on the return-risk pool. Phase 3: license the cancellation-cascade workflow to DMS and eContract vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody knows the real return rate. Everyone models it on Carvana's 7-day return, but the buyers who return are not typical, because the F&I office sees payment shock and buyer's remorse first. A 48-hour refund deadline is shorter than the time a lender, administrator or DMV normally takes to process anything, so the dealer's exposure is process failure, not vehicle depreciation. Whoever owns the process owns the data, and the data is what makes the insurance product priceable.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist by state and by lender for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents. Sell a $99 per month standby plan with a guaranteed 24-hour turnaround per return. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a shared spreadsheet and e-sign before writing any software. Log every step's time and dollar cost, since that log becomes the actuarial dataset.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ComplyAuto (exclusively licensed by CNCDA), CDK Global (DMS), CNCDA (California New Car Dealers Association), DealerCenter (DMS for independent dealers). White space: Research limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so no searches were run. That means no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches, and no search for startups by name. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch of about 30 primary and vendor URLs, with model-generated page summaries. I found NO dedicated 'unwind-as-a-service' for CARS Act cancellations, but I cannot rule out a small startup. Re-run the startup and forum searches before committing.

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

title: Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers
one_liner: A phone-based monthly proof-of-work ledger that turns gig, cash and self-employment activity into state-accepted documentation and 30-day cure packets, paid for by the Medicaid plans and health centers that lose revenue when members drop.
customer: Medicaid managed care organizations with expansion-adult lines, and FQHC and community health center networks. Medicaid is 43-50% of health center revenue, and an MCO is paid capitation per member-month. End users are expansion adults aged 19-64 with irregular income. The MCO or health center pays per retained member; the enrollee pays nothing.
problem: CMS's interim final rule (June 3, 2026) requires states to implement 80 hours a month of work or activity, or $580 a month in income, by Jan 1, 2027. Compliance is checked at application and at renewal, and a noncompliance notice gives 30 calendar days to cure. CBO projects about 4.8M coverage losses from work requirements, largely from reporting complexity. About 9 in 10 affected patients are expected to qualify for an exemption or already comply, yet many will still lose coverage on documentation. Nebraska went live May 1, 2026 with self-attestation, but about 28,000 people there must document twice a year and the state plans to move to verification.
solution: An enrollee-side SMS and app tool. It ingests bank and payment-app statements, gig platform earnings exports (Uber, DoorDash, Cash App, Venmo), pay stub photos and logged volunteer or class hours. It computes whether each month clears $580 or 80 hours and generates the state-specific verification packet. It sends look-back-month reminders and prepares the 30-day cure response. It flags likely exemption candidates, such as medically frail members, from plan claims data. The plan or clinic dashboard shows at-risk members and cure success. The tool only assists and never determines compliance, which is what federal rules allow plans to do.
why_now: The interim final rule was published June 3, 2026, and the national start date is Jan 1, 2027. Nebraska's live rollout is the preview of what other states will face when verification replaces self-attestation. CMS is encouraging automation, but states are spending on caseworker portals, notices and screening tools, not on income documentation for gig workers.
revenue_model: $3-8 per at-risk member per month billed to the MCO, or a success fee of $50-150 per member retained through renewal. FQHC SaaS at $2-5k per month per site with an outcomes dashboard. Later, state contracts for a self-employed and gig documentation module.
non_obvious_insight: Vendors such as Salesforce are building state-facing portals for applicants and caseworkers. The parties with a P&L at stake, the MCOs and health centers, are not yet being sold a member-side tool. KFF's roundup of state outreach plans covers notices, websites and screening tools but does not describe how self-employed or irregular income will be documented (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-federal-outreach-requirements-and-state-plans/). State wage-data matching misses 1099, cash and gig work by design. Georgetown's CCF warns that 'verification in this context means burdensome documentation requirements for enrollees' (https://ccf.georgetown.edu/2026/05/11/the-new-medicaid-work-reporting-requirements-are-here-dont-let-the-nebraska-soft-start-fool-you/). The retention math is lopsided: a plan or clinic can pay a few dollars a month per member to protect several hundred dollars of monthly revenue. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/03/2026-11094/medicaid-program-community-engagement-requirement-for-certain-individuals and https://www.pointcare.com/blog/how-to-prevent-medicaid-coverage-gaps-in-2026
first_30_days: Build the Nebraska flow first, since it is already live. Recruit 50 gig and self-employed Medicaid enrollees through one FQHC partner. Measure how many can produce a compliant $580 or 80-hour packet within 30 days. Take those results to two MCO member-engagement and quality leads for a paid pilot. Sign an LOI with one health center network before Jan 1, 2027.

title: SACCO-Financed Succession Desk, Paid on Milestones
one_liner: A white-label succession desk that payroll SACCOs offer their members: a check-off-repaid 'estate clearing loan' goes into a milestone escrow, and the company earns only as each case step is proven.
customer: The payer and channel is the mid-size payroll or sector SACCO (5k-100k members: teachers, health workers, county staff, police and prison staff) in central and western Kenya, sold to the CEO and credit committee. End users are two groups: salaried members (30-55) whose deceased parent's land is still in a dead name, and heirs of deceased members whose deposits and shares are stuck without a grant. The diaspora child is no longer the only payer.
problem: SACCOs hold two stuck pools. First, deposits and shares of deceased members that cannot be paid out cleanly until heirs produce a grant or agree among themselves (many SACCOs allow small nominee payouts; larger balances and family disputes stall; exact limits to verify): a governance headache, audit query and source of angry families. Second, living members who would borrow large development or mortgage loans against family land, but the land is in a dead person's name so the SACCO cannot take security. Members themselves cannot find a KES 100-250k lump sum for advocate, fees and travel, and distrust strangers who take money for land paperwork, yet they have salaries that can be deducted at source.
solution: The SACCO brands a 'Succession Desk'; the company runs it. Wedge (sellable in 30 days, no SACCO cash outlay): 'Deceased-Member Deposit Clearing'. The SACCO gives a letter of introduction and the list of stuck estates; the company does WhatsApp intake, heir map, consents and field work with a fixed-fee advocate panel; heirs consent in writing to a flat fee deducted from the released deposits. Stage 2, after three or more cases close: 'Estate Clearing Loan' for living members, sized KES 60-250k and repaid by payroll check-off. Proceeds sit in a SACCO-held milestone escrow released at proven steps: heir map and consent pack complete, petition filed and gazetted, confirmation of grant, transmission registered. Advocate fees (from a pre-agreed schedule) and the company's fee are paid from escrow to each party directly against milestones, so the member never hands cash to a stranger and the company never holds client money. At the end the SACCO has a pledgeable title (with heirs' consents to charge) and can pre-approve a development or mortgage loan.
why_now: Payroll SACCOs now run digital member ledgers, USSD and M-Pesa collections, and face competition from banks and digital lenders for their best salaried members, so they want secured, sticky products. Regulator attention on SACCO governance and deceased or dormant member balances (SASRA; verify current rules) makes stuck estates a board-level problem. LLM intake and heir mapping cut the cost of a case enough that a flat KES 12-18k fee works inside a loan. The succession backlog from 1960s-80s allottees is at its peak. Without cheap AI intake the desk would have needed paralegal armies, so this business model did not pencil out in 2019.
revenue_model: Contingent milestone fees of KES 12-18k per estate case, split over the four milestones (for example 40% at consents plus filing, 60% at grant and transmission), funded either from released deposits (deceased-member cases) or from estate clearing loan proceeds via escrow. The company takes no interest and no percentage of estate value. Flat per-loan bounty of KES 3-5k when a cleared title later secures a SACCO loan. After a successful pilot, a white-label desk fee of about KES 150-250k a year per SACCO. Illustration: 10 SACCOs at 100 cases a year each is roughly KES 15M in case fees plus about KES 2M in platform fees (about US$130k), with the SACCOs, not the company, carrying credit risk. The SACCO earns loan interest and clears a liability.
non_obvious_insight: Affordability and trust, not awareness, are the barriers, and the SACCO uniquely owns what neither an advocate nor a startup can: payroll check-off (repayment that costs almost nothing to collect), a welfare touchpoint at the exact moment of a death, and a balance-sheet motive (release stuck deposits, make land pledgeable). The estate clearing loan turns a scary lump sum into a monthly deduction, and the milestone escrow turns a scary stranger into a vendor who is only paid for proven progress. The SACCO's deceased-member float is an embarrassing liability nobody currently sells a fix for.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list 40 SACCOs whose managers you can reach through personal, church, alumni and county networks (teachers', hospital, county-staff SACCOs first). Ask one question: how many deceased-member accounts are pending succession and how many shillings are stuck? Days 10-20: sign two advocates to a fixed-fee panel schedule and draft a one-page pilot contract: SACCO letter of introduction, member-consented flat fee deducted from released deposits, no SACCO cash outlay, so it fits within a CEO's delegated authority and does not need a board vote. Days 20-30: sign one SACCO for 15-20 stuck estates, start intake on the first 5 by WhatsApp, and publish an anonymised 'stuck member deposits' figure to open the next SACCOs. In parallel, draft the estate clearing loan term sheet with that SACCO's credit committee. Metric: days from intake to consents complete, and shillings released per case.

title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Brownfield.ai, Scout (ScoutCities), LandGate, Enverus Site & Screen. White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k.

title: ERCOT Large-Load Energization Files, Fixed Fee
one_liner: A two-engineer Texas specialist that sells neocloud and colo developers a fixed-fee, six-week package of ISO-acceptable PSS/E and EMT models, a ride-through study and a compliance file, with a fee kicker paid when ERCOT accepts it.
customer: Wedge: VPs of power and interconnection leads at 30-60 mid-size neocloud, colo and AI-campus developers with 25-300 MW sites in ERCOT's large-load study queue, plus the EPCs that own their energization schedule. They have no in-house power-electronics staff. Hyperscalers with in-house power simulators are excluded on purpose.
problem: Since PGRR115 and NPRR1234 (effective late 2025), ERCOT wants studies and dynamic models for loads of 25 MW or more before energization. NOGRR282 (effective Aug 1, 2026) adds frequency and voltage ride-through requirements for large computational loads. A developer holds only OEM spec sheets. UPS and power-shelf control details sit behind OEM NDAs, and bespoke PSCAD consultants are slow and have never modeled a GPU power shelf. Every rejected model or resubmittal loop delays energization. At 100 MW of leased AI capacity, a month of slip defers roughly eight figures of rent or GPU revenue (rough estimate: about $100+/kW-month of critical IT), so a $150k package is a rounding error next to the delay it prevents.
solution:
Sell acceptance, not artifacts, in four steps.
1) A $15-25k gap analysis against the NOGRR282, PGRR115 and NPRR1234 texts, using the site's one-line diagram and UPS/PSU bill of materials.
2) A fixed-fee package of $90-180k: an ISO-submittable PSS/E dynamic model and EMT model, a ride-through and oscillation study, and a compliance file. It is built from reusable platform-level models of specific UPS, power-shelf and facility archetypes. Those models are HIL-validated at a partner lab (Typhoon HIL or OPAL-RT time, or a university lab) under OEM NDAs.
3) Submission handling and resubmittal support through ERCOT's large-load process.
4) A 25% success kicker paid on ERCOT acceptance, plus an annual re-issue subscription when GPU generation, UPS firmware or 800V DC changes the load.
why_now: NOGRR282 was approved July 9, 2026 and took effect Aug 1, 2026. PGRR115 (Nov and Dec 2025) and NPRR1234 (Dec 15, 2025) already gate energization on studies and models. The first wave of 25 MW and larger neocloud sites is hitting the queue now, before any consultancy has a large-load specialty. Rubin-generation hardware and 800V DC change the load behavior again within 12-18 months, which creates re-issue demand.
revenue_model: $15-25k gap analysis, $90-180k fixed-fee package, and a 25% success kicker on acceptance (about $25-45k). Add $20-40k per year model maintenance and re-issue per site, and later OEM test-and-listing fees for platform models. A year-1 target of about 12 packages at about $150k is roughly $1.8M with 2-3 engineers. Reuse of platform models across sites is what lifts gross margin past a consultancy's 30-40%.
non_obvious_insight: The developer does not want a model. It wants ERCOT's planners to sign off without a resubmittal loop. The durable business in inverter modeling after Blue Cut was not the model libraries, because vendors and ISOs published those. It was the shops that knew what the ISO's planners would accept. A single-regulator focus (ERCOT only) lets a two-person shop become the known acceptance expert in six months, and each accepted submission is precedent no generalist consultant has. Free generic EPRI or NERC models help us: they are conservative, and a developer who submits them risks being told to add buffer capacity or accept curtailment, while a product-specific validated model avoids that.
first_30_days: Week 1: read the actual NOGRR282 protocol text ('Large Electronic Load Ride-Through Requirements', 282NOGRR-01) and the PGRR115 and NPRR1234 submission forms. Call ERCOT large-load working group and planning contacts to confirm what compliance evidence is required. If it is self-attestation only, price down to gap analysis plus study and keep the acceptance-kicker idea for models only. Weeks 1-2: recruit one ex-ERCOT or TO planning engineer (Texas PE) and one power-electronics engineer, and publish an open ERCOT LCL Readiness Checklist. Weeks 2-4: work the public ERCOT large-load queue reports to list about 40 developers and the 10 biggest EPCs, and sell three $15k gap analyses. Sign a lab MOU and get a first UPS or power-shelf OEM NDA through the first paying customer's equipment.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Typhoon HIL (Data Centers solution), OPAL-RT (HYPERSIM, power-HIL), EPRI DCFlex, Emerald AI (Emerald Conductor). White space: Across this session's research I found no direct competitor selling packaged, hardware-validated large-load dynamic models (PSS/E plus EMT) with ride-through study reports and certification letters for GPU-cluster, PSU and UPS stacks. Nobody was seen selling OEM-level type-test certification for power shelves and UPS platforms. Adjacent players cover only pieces: HIL tools (Typhoon HIL, OPAL-RT), generic EMT consultancies, EPRI's flexibility consortium, workload-flex software (Emerald AI), and simulation software vendors with no data center library shown.

Three structural threats need answers:
1. Regulators and EPRI or NERC may publish free generic composite or EMT models, which commoditizes the model library.
2. OEMs (UPS, PSU, NVIDIA) own the confidential control details and may ship their own models.
3. Per-project EMT consulting already exists and is not verified either way for large loads.

The defensible white space is independent, hardware-validated, ISO-acceptable model packages and compliance evidence for the 25-500 MW neocloud and colo developers who lack in-house power simulators. It would be reused across sites through OEM platform type tests, not sold as bespoke studies.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before this task began, so competitor discovery relied on direct page fetches and GitHub search.
