Treat the 'no direct competitor' finding as moderate-confidence. Verify manually against NERC LLTF outputs, EPRI data center model reports, and WECC or ERCOT model requirements before committing. | How this version avoids them: Typhoon HIL and OPAL-RT are tool vendors, so we partner and buy their HIL time and they act as a channel. Electranix and Danovo do bespoke per-project studies for generators and transmission owners with no reusable GPU or UPS platform models and no ERCOT large-load precedent, and they are slower and costlier per site. EPRI DCFlex and free generic models are baselines we start from, not substitutes, because ERCOT wants site-specific and product-specific evidence. Emerald AI sells workload flexibility, whereas we sell compliance evidence for the fixed, fast-ramping load. Pearl Street speeds steady-state generation studies and has no dynamic large-load work. Hyperscaler in-house simulators are avoided by targeting only developers without them. Siemens PSS/E is the file format we deliver into, not a competitor.

title: Pumper-Sampled Hydrogen and Helium Ground-Truth Registry
one_liner: Stop digging through what the industry failed to measure and start measuring it: pay lease pumpers to grab wellhead gas samples, assay them for hydrogen and helium, and build the depth-tagged registry that becomes the standard for what is under the ground.
customer: Wedge: hydrogen, helium and geothermal explorers and their modelers (Koloma-type juniors outside their own acreage, HyTerra/MAX Power-type juniors, Terra AI, HyReveal) who commission sampling campaigns across a fairway. Contributors: small independent operators and the pumpers (lease operators) who visit each well weekly, starting with the Kansas and Oklahoma independents. Later payers: lenders, insurers and resource certifiers who need a standard, auditable measurement before they finance a discovery.
problem: Old well files are noisy for a structural reason: the industry never measured hydrogen or helium. Standard mud-logging and production gas analysis use flame-ionization detectors that cannot see H2 or He, so a 1935 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' note is an accident, contamination and sampling method are unknown, and the parent's archive is capped at about 16,000 free analyses and a 0.5% hit rate. Explorers who need to know where hydrogen and helium are today either drill blind, run private one-off campaigns, or use soil-gas anomalies. Nobody keeps a standardized, depth-tagged, contamination-corrected, fresh measurement for the roughly one million producing US wells or the tens of thousands of new holes drilled each year.
solution: A three-layer business. Layer 1 (first product, sellable in 6 months): buyer-commissioned sampling campaigns. A buyer specifies a transect or 200-well fairway; operators allow their pumpers to fill a $12 sample container at the casinghead or separator vent following a safety protocol; a bounty of about $25 goes to the pumper; samples go to a partner lab or an in-house GC-TCD unit, and the buyer gets H2/He/N2/CO2/Ar/O2/C1-C6 with GPS, photo, chain of custody and an air-contamination correction. Layer 2: a registry with an open measurement spec (sampling method, contamination QC, lab certification) and a contribution scheme: operators get a free full gas assay (which many already pay $50-150 for to support BTU, sales or flaring reports, a hypothesis to test), exclusive rights to their own well results for 90-180 days, and a revenue share. Layer 3: a certified add-on H2/He TCD channel for mud-logging contractors and geothermal drillers so every new hole feeds the registry, and a scoring layer that uses fresh samples to calibrate the archive-based confidence grades from the parent idea.
why_now: Hydrogen and helium explorers are funded (Koloma about $245M, Mantle8 EUR31M, Terra AI $20M with BHP and Khosla, 123 companies per AKAP) but starved of trustworthy labels, and the modelers (Terra AI, HyReveal) explicitly need fresh ground-truth data. Portable micro-GC/TCD analyzers and smartphone chain-of-custody have made distributed sampling cheap, and VLM tools make the old archive a cheap starting prior rather than the product. Geothermal and helium buyers want auditable data for financing, and no standard exists yet, which is the moment a standard can be set.
revenue_model: Sampling campaigns at about $250 per well (cost roughly $60-120 with in-house GC and $130-170 with outside labs); a 200-well campaign is about $50k. Registry subscriptions of $10-50k per basin per year for explorers and modelers. Data licenses to modelers and financiers. Lab certification and channel fees from mud-logging contractors. Optional later: small overriding royalties on leases taken over registry-flagged sections. Year-1 target: 1,500-3,000 wells sampled, 5-8 campaign customers (about $300-400k), 10 registry subscribers.
non_obvious_insight: The right inversion is that data quality, not data availability, is the bottleneck: every archive layer the parent proposed is limited by a measurement nobody made. Because operators pay for gas analysis anyway, the marginal cost of adding H2 and He to a routine sample is almost zero, so the contributor network can be built with a bounty rather than a salesforce. The registry's moat is network economics plus a standard: contributors are also the sources, the modelers need the labels, and lenders will trust the one dataset with certified provenance. Fresh samples also calibrate the archive-derived confidence scores, so the parent idea becomes a cheap prior on top of a proprietary ground-truth set.
first_30_days: Week 1: contract a commercial gas lab that runs GC-TCD (or buy a used micro-GC with TCD for about $15-25k) and design the sample kit and safety protocol with an experienced pumper. Week 2: sign 2 independent operators (about 100 wells each, via the Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association and personal referrals) on the free-assay, 90-day-exclusive deal. Week 3: sample 100 wells across a transect crossing the Nemaha uplift and publish a one-page ground-truth map. Week 4: pitch 15 juniors and modelers a 200-well campaign at $250 per well with half prepaid, and ask HyReveal and Terra AI for a data-partner letter. Kill test: if no buyer prepays by week 6, sell the same samples as a section-level pack to landmen (see the sharpened offspring).

Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar: proprietary data only in their own footprints; they become campaign buyers outside their acreage. Terra AI and HyReveal: modelers who lack labels, so they are customers and channel partners rather than competitors. title: Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors
one_liner: Sell seed VCs, pharma BD teams and AI-bio founders confidential 'does this paper's key result actually work?' intelligence, from anonymous postdoc consensus polls up to paid replication of the one key experiment.
customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms, pharma BD and scouting teams evaluating academic spinouts or in-licensing, and AI-bio startups building on published wet-lab claims. Pay $4-6k for a poll-only memo and $15-40k for a key-experiment replication.
problem: Investors and BD teams can't tell which high-profile papers replicate. The truth exists as hallway consensus: 'that result only works in the first author's hands', 'nobody outside that lab can get the organoid protocol to run', 'cells were cultured as previously described' with four layers of citations. Formal diligence hires KOL consultants who are conflicted and often the PI's friends, or a CRO that needs 4 months and a full protocol. Bad academic-asset bets burn $5-20M before anyone notices.
solution: Wedge product 'Bench Pulse': in 5 business days, poll 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous postdocs and senior techs working in the exact subfield about the named claim, reagents and protocol. Deliver a structured memo with consensus, red flags, the Figure-3 problem, which reagents or lots are fragile, and a 'what to test first' plan. Upsell: 'Key-Figure Replication'. A pool of laid-off or between-position scientists runs the single decisive experiment in 3-4 weeks in rented bench space (not on university property), with pre-registered success criteria and blinded readout.
why_now: Biotech funding since 2023 rewards capital efficiency, so seed funds want cheaper, faster kill decisions. Pharma is shopping for early assets in academia and abroad. AI-bio companies are building on published wet-lab claims with little bench sense. NIH disruption and biotech layoffs have released a large pool of very good bench scientists who want paid, flexible work. Expert-network compliance norms are now well understood, so a compliant structure is feasible.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee per poll memo and per replication study. Annual retainer for funds that want a pipeline-wide 'bench pulse' (about $30-60k). Optional success-fee or advisory equity for AI-bio startups.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not lab capacity, it is candid consensus. Replication is expensive, but the postdoc informal network already knows which labs' results hold up. The winning move is to monetize that gossip compliantly and only spend on replication after the poll narrows the question. GLG-style expert calls fail because they interview one conflicted senior person instead of 10 juniors who actually do the pipetting.
first_30_days: Choose one subfield you personally have 20 contacts in (for example CAR-T, organoids, targeted protein degradation or spatial biology). Build the compliant NDA plus anonymity protocol with a lawyer for about $3k. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on one asset they are already looking at. Convert the fund that reacts to a paid $5k poll, then upsell one replication. Pay panelists $150-300 per poll from the first revenue.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hoeford Research, Alacrita, Fios Genomics, GLG. White space: Caveat on coverage: the WebSearch quota was exhausted (200 of 200) before this task started. I substituted direct WebFetch of competitor pages, Google News RSS, and some Brave and Bing queries. Brave rate-limited me (429) and Bing returned junk. Hoeford and Fios pages were blocked or truncated. So 'nothing found' is weaker than a full sweep, and the founder should confirm with Crunchbase and LinkedIn plus 10 calls to seed VCs.

What I found. Both halves of the idea have adjacent players, but I found no one selling the specific product as described.

Poll half. Expert networks (GLG, Guidepoint, Third Bridge) and scientific-diligence boutiques (Alacrita, Fios) all sell expert input to investors. They interview senior experts and KOLs, sell bespoke projects, and market to finance clients. I found no fixed-price, 5-day, named-claim consensus poll of 8-15 anonymous junior bench scientists. That is a real wedge, and it fits the founder's critique that the incumbents rely on conflicted seniors.

Replication half. 'Wet diligence' at CROs or independent labs is an accepted practice (LifeSciVC says it should be 'gating before investing'). Hoeford appears to sell it. Science Exchange has the marketplace and the history (Reproducibility Initiative, RP:CB). The bundle, where the poll narrows the question and then a pre-registered, blinded replication follows, looks unserved. Owning a bench pool of laid-off scientists is the least defensible and most operationally risky part.

Segment. AI-bio founders building on published wet-lab claims are the least served, but Adaptyv Bio (raised $40M, 3-week assays from $149 per protein) is already serving protein-design validation.

Structural threats.
- GLG or Guidepoint can copy the poll cheaply once it is proven, since they already sell surveys.
- Anonymity is leaky in subfields of 20-50 people.
- Postdocs risk their careers and may breach university confidentiality or employment terms.
- A negative poll about a named PI's paper carries defamation and tortious-interference exposure.
- A replication that fails in a new lab does not prove the claim is false, which is the ambiguity buyers hate.

title: Tooling Title Diligence for Small-Brand Acquirers
one_liner: A fixed-fee, 5-day report that tells buyers of $2M-$50M product companies which molds the target legally owns, where they physically sit, and whether the factory is already selling the target's product.
customer: Buyers of physical-product brands and small manufacturers with China-made tooling: search-fund and ETA searchers, independent sponsors, lower-mid-market PE platforms and SBA 7(a) acquirers. The channel is business brokers (Quiet Light, Empire Flippers, FE International-type firms), M&A attorneys and SBA acquisition lenders. The payer is the buyer, at the LOI-to-close stage. Secondary payer is the seller, who pays for a pre-listing 'tooling-ready' file.
problem: In a small-brand acquisition the molds are the asset that everyone values at zero. The QoE accountant sees an expensed PO line, the lawyer sees a boilerplate 'all assets used in the business' rep, and the seller often cannot say whose name the tools are in or whether a bill of sale exists. If the factory holds the tools, the buyer has bought a business that the supplier can hold hostage for a 30% price hike, and the buyer also cannot move production, which matters more now that tariff rules keep changing. Nobody in the deal owns this question: brand-protection vendors sell to the brand, not to the buyer, and audit firms do not cover tooling.
solution: 'Tooling Title and Leakage Report', delivered in 5 business days. (1) Tool schedule: every tool, its location, its condition, and who holds title (bill of sale, PO language, tool-ownership clauses, supplier confirmation letters). (2) Leakage test, which is the parent's $2,500 overrun audit repurposed: buy 10 units from 1688, Alibaba, Temu and Amazon third-party sellers, and compare them with the golden sample and lot codes to say whether the supplier is already selling the product. (3) Portability score: what it would cost and how long it would take to move each tool or re-cut it, with quotes from a US or Mexican molder. (4) Deal remedies: draft closing conditions, a tool bill-of-sale assignment, custody and release agreements, and a holdback or escrow sizing suggestion for the buyer's lawyer to use. The on-site audit is optional and subcontracted, passed through at cost, and only for deals over $10M.
why_now: The searcher and ETA wave and retiring owners are pushing more small manufacturers and brands to market. The Amazon aggregator unwinding put many product brands up for resale with tooling and supplier problems. Tariff volatility (the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling per the parent research) makes 'can this brand switch factories?' a live diligence question, where in 2019 it was rarely asked. Remote marketplace scanning has become cheap enough to fit inside a fixed fee.
revenue_model: $4,900 per report, paid by the buyer, usually as a closing cost. Seller pre-listing file $2,500 through brokers. Post-close '100-day tool sovereignty plan' $12k (title cure, fingerprint baseline, second-source quotes). Portfolio monitoring for PE sponsors $2,000/month per physical-product company. Model: 240 reports a year at month 12 is about $1.2M, plus a 25% attach rate on the plan (60 plans at $12k) is about $0.7M. Reachable market is assumed at roughly 1,500 physical-product deals a year, to be validated with brokers. Lenders or brokers might pay for reports on deals that later close.
non_obvious_insight: This is the same asset as the parent idea, but a far better moment to sell it. A breakup victim only hires you once they are already hurt and have already lost leverage. An acquirer is at peak willingness to pay, because they are about to wire $5M, and the report's cost is rounding error on the deal. The finding also turns straight into money: a missing bill of sale becomes a closing condition, a holdback or a price cut. A short-lived supplier concentration risk becomes a negotiating chip. Diligence is also the top of a repeat-customer funnel, since a sponsor with 6 platform companies buys monitoring on all of them.
first_30_days: Build a redacted sample report from public listings and a mock data room. Pitch 6 brokers and 3 searcher communities, offering 3 free reports on live deals, in exchange for testimonials and a written referral agreement, since a diligence step that reduces buyer fear helps brokers close deals. Then sell 5 paid reports at an introductory $3,500. Get one M&A attorney to endorse the closing-condition language. Line up two China audit contractors by referral for the on-site option. Kill signal: brokers refuse to introduce the report to buyers, or no buyer will pay $3.5k.

The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. If the part is generic or unbranded, a match proves little. Harris Sliwoski sells legal hours after a dispute, so we are the fact base their M&A-side peers lack. Alitheon and MoldTrax do not play in deal timelines. Sourcify is a natural post-close channel for the re-sourcing step. Accounting-based QoE and general legal diligence firms are the real adjacent substitutes, and they do not physically verify tools or test the marketplace (assumption, to check in the 20 first conversations).

title: Subpoena-Ready Rate Cards for Lien-Based Clinics
one_liner: Invert the parent by selling the coder bench to the clinics being attacked, using their own ledgers to defend their prices and build the industry's only record of what LOP care actually collects.
customer: Owner-operators of multi-location chiropractic groups, pain-management practices, ortho groups and physician-owned ASCs in Florida, Texas and Georgia that treat on letters of protection, especially those who have just received a subpoena or whose plaintiff-firm partners ask for 'defensible bills'. Wedge is 3-15 location groups in Houston, Atlanta, Orlando, Tampa and Miami. Plaintiff-firm referral managers act as influencers and channel.
problem: Reform made a clinic's pricing method, LOP arrangements, factoring and referral relationships discoverable. Owners are now deposed on how they priced a CPT code, and 'it is our standard rate' loses against a chart showing 8-15x Medicare. The honest answer is that LOP care is a credit product. The clinic waits 12-24 months, bears loss risk and often writes off 30-60% blindly at settlement. That premium is legitimate but undocumented, and nobody derives it from the clinic's own ledger. Plaintiff lawyers are not billing experts, and today's billing experts are hired after the attack.
solution: Product: LOP rate-card defense. (1) Ledger study: ingest 24-36 months of the clinic's LOP AR ledger from its practice-management export, computing realized collection per billed dollar, time-to-cash and non-recovery by code, attorney and venue. (2) Cost-of-carry model: derive a documented deferred-payment and collection-risk premium from that data. (3) Rate-card rebuild: restructure the fee schedule to a stated formula (local commercial median from payer Transparency-in-Coverage files times the documented premium) with coding hygiene fixes, written up in a dated, contemporaneous methodology memo signed by a certified coder and a health economist or CPA. (4) Deposition-defense packet for the owner and a ready declaration. (5) Annual attestation, quarterly drift check, and a per-bill 'rate-card attestation' clinics can attach. Scope excludes anything that hides referral or funding relationships. Disclosure remains counsel's job, and a healthcare regulatory lawyer reviews the offer for anti-kickback and fee-splitting risk.
why_now: Florida cases post-2023 and Georgia cases post-2025 are producing the first wave of provider subpoenas and depositions about rate-setting and referral relationships. Messy practice-management exports can now be normalized cheaply with LLMs, and payer Transparency-in-Coverage files make a local commercial median computable for free. Neither existed at usable cost in 2019.
revenue_model: Ledger X-ray free. Rate-card study $6.5k one-time. Monitoring and attestation $750-1,500/month per practice. Deposition prep $250/hr. Illustration: 100 clinics at $6.5k plus $900/month is about $1.7M in year one. The 10x layer is data and standard. After 150+ clinics and 30 months of ledgers, publish a quarterly 'LOP Realized Value Index' (free summary, paid detail) sold to carriers, funders, reinsurers and legislators, plus a registry that carriers pay to query. Carriers that agree to a fast lane for attested bills within the index band create a private fee schedule for the schedule-less LOP world, the way workers' comp fee schedules replaced price fights. Balance-sheet optionality later is a fund that buys attested receivables at index-based prices.
non_obvious_insight: The best defense of an LOP bill is explaining why it is what it is, not proving it is cheap, and the party holding the most valuable data on real LOP value is the clinic, not the carrier or the lawyer. Selling to the attacked party is the cheapest way to acquire that data, since a subpoena is a fear purchase with budget behind it. Providers will hand ledgers to a neutral appraiser but never to a carrier vendor, which is counter-positioning that Enlyte and CLARA cannot copy without alienating carriers. The credibility risk is issuer-pays conflict, mitigated by algorithmic pass/fail thresholds, a published methodology, a visible fail rate, a carrier-side advisory seat and a firewall from any case-specific testimony.
first_30_days: Pick Houston and Orlando/Tampa. Build a list of 60 lien-based groups from provider directories and plaintiff-firm referral networks, and approach through state chiropractic and pain-medicine associations and referral managers at plaintiff firms. Offer the free 'ledger X-ray': send an AR export and in 5 days get a one-page showing billed versus collected, time-to-cash and the five lines an expert would attack first. Sign 5 paid studies at $6.5k within 60 days. In parallel, hold 3 carrier claims-executive calls to test whether an attested schedule would be accepted in pre-suit, and one call with a healthcare regulatory attorney on structure and disclaimers.
lineage: mutation of I0428 ('Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions, FAIR Health, EvenUp, Turquoise Health. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files. | How this version avoids them: Enlyte and CLARA serve carriers and cannot sell to providers without channel conflict, and providers will not share ledgers with them. FAIR Health measures charges and allowed amounts, while we measure realized LOP collections and carry cost, so the index complements it and rebuts the plaintiff's usual-and-customary anchor. EvenUp is plaintiff-side treatment and demand software with no rate-card defense and is a possible channel partner for its firms' referral networks. Turquoise does payer-contracting analytics, not lien care, and is a data supplier with some entrant risk to watch. The closest direct substitute is per-case billing experts (including plaintiff-side JurisPro-type experts). They are hired after the attack and sell single-case declarations, while this is contemporaneous, subscription-based, data-backed documentation that carries more weight than a declaration created after the fact.

title: Consent Ledger for Land-Scheme Family Cohorts
one_liner: A cohort-priced heir-consent ledger sold to the family 'treasurer' of heirs from ONE 1960s-80s land-buying company or settlement scheme, with a partner law firm as the legal entity of record and a recurring Title Watch on top.
customer: The 'family treasurer': the salaried eldest or most solvent sibling (30-55, in Nairobi, Nakuru, Dallas or Dubai) of a family whose parent or grandparent was an allottee or member of one named land-buying company or settlement scheme in one county (pick one scheme in Murang'a, Kiambu, Nakuru or Trans Nzoia through the founder's own church/alumni/clan network). Distribution partners are the scheme's officials and welfare committee. One partner law firm is the entity of record for all legal work.
problem: Judges flagged three flaws in the parent: thin unit economics (field trips per single estate eat the KES 15-25k fee), the Advocates Act risk of a non-lawyer company selling a 'court-ready bundle' (from memory, unverified), and unproven diaspora willingness to pay. The underlying pain is real but narrower than 'succession': the blocker is proving that all 8-20 heirs were found, asked and agreed, and getting them to sign at all. There is also a sharper trigger than paperwork guilt: land in a dead man's name is an easy target for forged transfers and brokers, and absent children fear waking up to find it sold. A generic 'succession kit' has neither the density to be profitable nor a legal shape that survives scrutiny.
solution: Three steps, each cheap to buy. (0) 'Title Check', KES 1,500 over WhatsApp: photo of the title or parcel number, official search (about KES 500 fee, verify), LLM read of the result, one-page plain-language answer: registered owner, is that person dead, who must be involved. (1) 'Consent Ledger', KES 18k (KES 14k cohort price when 8+ estates from the same chief's location are booked): Kenyan name-variant-reconciled heir map, list of required consents, and a live status board the treasurer shares in the family WhatsApp group ('9 of 14 heirs signed, 3 outstanding, reasons'). A home-area agent runs one scheduled 'signing day' per chief's location per month for chief's-letter requests, ID copies, thumbprints and video consent; heirs elsewhere sign by ID-video on WhatsApp witnessed by the nearest agent. Output is a non-legal 'Consent and Kinship Evidence Pack' with a dispute flag (silent heir, second household, contested claim). The partner law firm receives the pack through a case-management seat, drafts, files and shepherds the case, and bills its own scale fee directly; the company never drafts affidavits or quotes legal fees. (2) 'Title Watch', KES 4k per parcel per year: alerts on registry changes plus a caution/restriction workflow run through the advocate. Asset discovery (SACCO, coop, UFAA letters) is a flat add-on sold only after grant, since UFAA beneficiary claims need the confirmed grant first.
why_now: LLMs now read scanned titles, IDs and share certificates and reconcile Kenyan name variants for cents a page, and drafting copilots (Wakili-Intel appeared July 2026 as a hobby project) are commoditising the paperwork, so the scarce, defensible piece moves to field evidence and multi-heir consent, which is still custom work. The settlement-scheme allottee generation is dying now. WhatsApp Business plus M-Pesa/card make small cross-border payments routine, and digitised searches (Ardhisasa; coverage to be verified) cut registry running. None of this worked in 2019: reading messy scans and chatting in Swahili and English at this cost did not exist.
revenue_model: Ladder per estate: KES 1.5k Title Check, then KES 18k ledger (14k at cohort density), then KES 3k flat advocate seat fee per file (software and case management charge, explicitly not a fee split; verify with counsel), then KES 4k/yr Title Watch, then KES 5k asset-discovery add-on after grant. Assumption to test: at cohort density, field plus search plus ops cost is about KES 7-8k per ledger versus KES 12-15k for one-off estates, giving roughly 45-55% gross margin and about KES 26-30k first-year revenue per estate. A county team (coordinator, 2 agents, share of ops, about KES 3M a year) breaks even near 200 estates a year, which one large scheme can supply. Title Watch gives recurring revenue that the parent lacked.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of production is not the estate but the chief's location. Neighbouring estates in one scheme share the same registry, chief, original allottee list, surnames and often the same feuds, so every ledger makes the next one cheaper and better (name-variant dictionary, known-disputer flags, chief relationships). That density economy is invisible to per-estate advocates and to national software. Second, the treasurer is buying a status board, not paperwork: it turns family guilt and pressure into visible progress that nudges holdout siblings. Third, fear of land-grabbing is the purchase trigger, so sell 'protect it' first and 'sort the succession' second.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pick one scheme and one county through your own family, church or alumni network; sign one partner law firm as entity of record on a one-page engagement letter (advocate bills the client directly; company charges a flat seat fee). Days 7-20: launch the WhatsApp 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' Title Check at KES 1,500 in the scheme's clan and welfare WhatsApp groups and in diaspora groups for that county; run 40 checks. Days 20-30: convert to 10 pre-sold Consent Ledgers at pilot price, of which at least 8 in one chief's location; schedule the first group signing day. Core metrics: days from intake to all heirs signed, percent of heirs signed on the first visit, and check-to-ledger conversion. Kill test: fewer than 3 of 40 checkers buy a ledger.
lineage: mutation of I0474 ('Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Luru (open-source 'Kenya's Digital Succession Copilot'), Wakili-Intel (AI drafting copilot for Kenyan advocates), Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority (UFAA), Ardhisasa (Ministry of Lands digital land registry). White space: Provisional, because the web search budget hit its 200-call cap before any search returned results. My evidence comes only from direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches. I found no funded startup, product or open-source project that combines (a) diaspora-paid flat-fee intake, (b) heir mapping across Kenyan name variants, (c) field-agent collection of chief's letters and thumbprint or video consent from 8-20 relatives, and (d) hand-off to partner advocates. The unserved wedge is the coordination and evidence-gathering layer sold to the paying sibling abroad. It is still unproven whether ordinary advocates or land-buying-company agents already do this informally, because I could not search for them. | How this version avoids them: Fixed-fee advocates (the only direct competitor) become the channel: they receive consent-complete, dispute-triaged files at zero acquisition cost and keep all legal fees, while the company sells only the field and evidence layer they cannot profitably do at scale fees (chasing 14 heirs across three counties). Luru and Wakili-Intel are zero-star software with no field agents, consent capture or advocates, and drafting is exactly what we do not sell. UFAA is used only after grant as a flat add-on, not a lead product. Ardhisasa and court e-filing are systems we file into, not substitutes; even if Ardhisasa adds guided transmission it will not collect thumbprints from scattered heirs. Defensibility comes from cohort density and the per-scheme kinship dictionary (cornered resource) plus counter-positioning against advocates who cannot make per-heir chasing pay.

title: Neutral Registry and Standard for Neighbor Baselines
one_liner: An independent, vendor-agnostic registry and open protocol that notarizes pre-construction baselines from any sensor vendor or consultant, gets referenced in county ordinances and a model presumption statute, and becomes the title-plant-style record that insurers and lenders underwrite against.
customer: Three payers, sequenced. (1) Sensor vendors and developer-hired consultancies (KETOS, Aethair, Kunak resellers, TRC and Salas O'Brien-type firms) that need a neutral stamp so counties will believe their data. (2) Data center developers who must file a baseline to satisfy an ordinance or a hearing (50-500 MW campuses in contested counties). (3) Later, insurers, lenders and state agencies buying registry data and certification. Counties and regulators are the standard's adopters, not payers.
problem: Every county and agency is inventing its own baseline rules: a 48-hour ambient sound survey here, monitoring wells and a hydrogeologist there (Franklin County IN, Chadds Ford PA, Shenandoah VA, St. Louis, Virginia DEQ's five Kunak sensors in Loudoun). Developer-hired consultants produce the data, so residents distrust it; opposition-side groups produce competing data, so developers distrust that. Nothing makes a baseline tamper-evident, comparable across sites, or legally meaningful. Unlike Pennsylvania's Act 13 for oil and gas (operators pay for pre-drill tests, and a rebuttable presumption applies when no baseline exists), no data-center equivalent creates a legal reason to buy, which is the parent's biggest unproven assumption.
solution: Build the audit-firm layer for baselines, in four steps. (1) Protocol v1, open and free: sensor siting rules, control-site design, QA/QC, minimum 90 days pre-application, chain of custody and data schema for wells, noise, PM2.5 and voltage, written with a land-grant university hydrogeologist and an acoustician. (2) The registry: any vendor submits raw data through an API, and we run automated QA, protocol audit and dual-key custody (a university library or state geological survey as second custodian, plus RFC 3161-style public timestamp logs, no token). The output is a Registered Baseline certificate with tamper-evident, first-in timestamps and a public read-only view. (3) The adoption engine: a one-page ordinance rider ('baseline must be registered under an independent public-benefit protocol') sent to every county drafting rules, and a model bill for the January 2027 legislative sessions (TX and NY are the pressure points) that adapts the Act 13 logic: a registered baseline lets a developer rebut unsupported claims, while no registered baseline shifts the presumption to the operator. (4) Governance: a public-benefit board with county, university, developer and resident seats, so no vendor controls it. Year 2-3 balance-sheet option: once 30+ campuses are registered, use the loss-relevant data to launch a developer-owned risk retention group or mutual for neighbor-harm guarantees, with the registry as its underwriting file. The same registry then extends to other large-load neighbors (battery storage, fabs, lithium, hydrogen).
why_now: The moratorium wave (NY EO 62 on July 14, Texas TCEQ halt on Sept 21, local pauses) means regulators must define 'what evidence counts' before lifting pauses. State legislatures convene in January 2027. Counties are copy-pasting bespoke baseline language right now, so an early standard can be the copied text. Public-sector baselines are starting (Virginia DEQ's Loudoun air sensors since Feb 2026) and need tamper-evident custody, and the Newton County lawsuit (Sept 2026) is a live example of dueling studies. Sensor prices collapsed, so the scarce input is now trust, not data.
revenue_model: Registry filing fee of $15-25k per site (protocol audit, QA, dual-key custody, certificate) plus $3-6k per year custody for 10 years; vendor and assessor certification of about $10k per firm per year for the registry-verified listing; data and API licences to insurers, lenders, state agencies and researchers; later, a premium share if a mutual launches. Bottom-up sketch: 150 new registrations per year at $20k = $3M; 500 custodied sites at $4.5k = $2.25M; 60 certified firms at $10k = $0.6M; about $6M per year by year 3 from data centers alone, with the upside from adjacent industries and underwriting data. Sales-cycle proxy: a filing is a line item in a permit budget, not a new budget.
non_obvious_insight: The incumbents are the channel, not the enemy. Developer-hired consultants and sensor vendors already produce the baselines but cannot be believed, and their best sales asset is a credible neutral attestation, exactly as companies prepare their own books but need an independent auditor to be trusted. So the registry sells to the competitors' customers through the competitors, and vendors pay to be certified because counties will ask for it. The moat is a cornered resource (first-in timestamped pre-construction baselines cannot be recreated after a site is built), network economies (cross-site data improves control models and expected-loss estimates) and switching costs (10-year custody), backed by counter-positioning (a vendor cannot be neutral without giving up its own product). The lever that decides everything is the legal presumption, which is why the model bill and ordinance rider are part of the product, not lobbying on the side.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: draft Protocol v0.1 with a land-grant extension hydrogeologist and an independent acoustician; publish it CC-BY with a one-page ordinance rider. Days 10-25: send the rider to the county attorneys behind Franklin County IN, Shenandoah VA, Chadds Ford PA and 10 other counties with open drafts; ask to be named as an acceptable registry. Days 15-30: sign 3-5 letters of intent from sensor vendors and consultancies to submit pilot baselines for the Registered Baseline certificate; book calls with two state association-of-counties or legislative staff on presumption language for TX and NY. Sell the first two filings ($12-18k pilot pricing) to developers with hearings in the next 60-90 days. Six-month target: 10 registered sites, 3 vendors certified, one ordinance or permit condition naming the registry, $150-250k of fees. Gate: if no county or regulator will reference the protocol within 6 months, fall back to selling attestations as a service inside the well-trustee model (offspring 1).
lineage: mutation of I1172 ('Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence. | How this version avoids them: It does not compete with KETOS, Aethair, Kunak, Clarity, Larson Davis or Eno on hardware or dashboards; they submit data and pay to be verified, so their marketing (KETOS's 'missing baseline', Aethair's pre-construction guide) creates our demand. Envirosuite, the strongest incumbent, sells recurring monitoring SaaS to sites that pay it and cannot credibly be the independent notary of its own customers' data. Consultancies (TRC, Salas O'Brien, Trinity, SCS) are developer-hired and gain from a stamp that makes their work believed. CEDS advises opposition groups and is not neutral, but its recommended pre-, during- and post-construction baselines match our protocol, so it is a natural endorser. Prevolt and Jambo sell engagement and risk screens, not evidence custody. Developer substitutes (checks, buyouts, pledges) are unrelated budgets. No standard-setting registry for data-center baselines surfaced in the parent's research or in a fresh search of ordinances and guidance, which showed bespoke county-by-county language.

title: Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel
one_liner: Turn the ~55 GW of idle data center backup generators into dispatchable capacity by solving the air-permit problem instead of the hardware problem.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets. Secondary buyers are utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Data centers hold about 55 GW of backup diesel (Virginia alone has about 27 GW permitted), and it runs 10-30 minutes a month. PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring their own capacity or be curtailed. Air permits cap non-emergency run hours, so nobody can legally count these engines as capacity.
solution: Fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' packages. They cover a state-specific permit modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits), engineering and financing for emissions retrofits on the subset of engines that need them, and paralleling/telemetry upgrades. Enrollment in PJM's on-site backup (IRAS-style) and demand-response programs comes with third-party measurement and verification. Runtime is capped at a few dozen to ~100 hours a year, dispatched only in system emergencies, with community disclosure built in.
why_now: PJM's July auction shortfall, the proposed backstop auction (15-year terms, $555/MW-day cap) and the curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule make backup generation valuable for the first time. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so this fleet is the only large block of capacity that exists today.
revenue_model: $40-150k fixed fee per site for permit and engineering work, plus 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the $325/MW-day cap a 20 MW fleet is worth very roughly $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fee is easy to justify. Retrofit financing adds a spread.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest big block of new PJM capacity is not new. It is already built and sitting behind a fence, and the barrier is air-permit lawyering that VC-backed hardware companies ignore. A repeatable per-state permit playbook is the moat. Emergency-only runtime is why it works: at under 1% of hours, the capacity value dwarfs the emissions.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permit files for ~30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL. Build a 'permit headroom map' showing run-hour caps and engine tiers. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit of a 20+ MW fleet and aim to close two paid pilots.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead.

title: Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores
one_liner: Evidence packs showing a coarse satellite-derived wildfire score is wrong about one specific lot, filed under new statutory appeal rights.
customer: Independent insurance agents and HOAs or fire-safe councils in Colorado and California whose clients face nonrenewal or surcharges. Insurers' appeal desks are a later buyer.
problem: Colorado HB25-1182 (in force since July 1, 2026) makes insurers disclose the parcel's score, credit documented mitigation and offer an appeal. California AB 75, operative July 1, 2026, gives notice and dispute rights over aerial-imagery nonrenewals. But 'owners still have to prove their case', and many wildfire models lean on roughly 30 m fuel layers and stale imagery that misclassify irrigated, gravel-scaped or recently cleared lots.
solution: For each parcel, pull the disclosed model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density, distance to wildland) and overlay multi-date 15-50 cm satellite imagery showing vegetation change, roof material and clearance, plus dated homeowner photos. Produce a regulator-format rebuttal pack with a ranked list of cheap fixes, and give agents a dashboard that scans their whole book for likely score errors. The real edge is a growing database of which input errors insurers concede.
why_now: Both disclosure-and-appeal regimes went live in July 2026 and insurers' appeal desks are unprepared. Commercial constellations, including 30 cm Pelican and Vantor archives, plus 15 cm HD, have made high-resolution archives cheap. Regulators in CT, NH and PA say imagery alone is insufficient, and NY has a pending bill.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per parcel via agents. $10-$25 per parcel per year for HOA book scans. About $60 per appeal from insurers for standardised evidence intake.
non_obvious_insight: Wildfire scores are averages of coarse layers, so the cheapest way to change a score is often to fix an input error rather than harden the house. The resolution gap between 30 m models and 30 cm imagery is systematic, so a win on one lot tends to generalise to its neighbours and compounds into a book-level lever for agents.
first_30_days: Pick the Colorado Front Range. Recruit 5 independent agencies with 200+ WUI clients each, plus 2 HOAs. Run the first 50 score disclosures at a $99 pilot price per file, and track appeal success rate as the marketing asset.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: FireRisk.ai (RiskIntel AI), DefensibleHome Wildfire Insurance Survival Kit, Defensible Space Score (AACI Group / Five Bays Insurance Agency), Road Home Exteriors 'insurance-grade verification packets'. White space: Nobody found sells imagery-based, parcel-level, insurer-format rebuttal evidence, and nobody sells an agent or HOA 'scan the whole book for likely score errors' workflow. What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery.

title: Same-Week MFP Refunds for Senior-Care Pharmacies
one_liner: A refund-purchase facility for independent long-term-care pharmacies that becomes the payee of record on Medicare's negotiated-price refunds and pays out within two business days, underwritten claim by claim.
customer: Owners and CFOs of independent closed-door long-term-care (LTC) and senior-living pharmacies, and groups of 3-30 of them. First reached through the Senior Care Pharmacy Coalition, whose members warned that 60% may close in 2026 without a fix. Our estimate, to be checked against real claims exports, is a float of $150k to $1M+ per LTC pharmacy (Eliquis, Xarelto, Jardiance, Januvia, Farxiga and Entresto dominate senior volume). That is 5-30x the $27k a month NCPA cites for an average community pharmacy, so each logo is worth far more.
problem: LTC pharmacies pay wholesalers full price on a 7-14 day cycle and then wait about 21 days (CMS/MTF average; 67% of NCPA respondents wait 22+ days) for the difference between price and Maximum Fair Price. They already carry slow nursing-home and PBM receivables. Their bank has a blanket lien and almost certainly treats a non-trade manufacturer refund as ineligible collateral, so the refund float is funded from owner savings or by cutting stock of the drugs seniors need. Merchant cash advances cost far too much for a stream that is statutory.
solution: 1) Onboard with 8-12 weeks of PMS claims exports and MTF remittance files. The free 'refund aging and dilution audit' is our underwriting diligence, not the product. 2) Make the refund land where we control it. Preferred route is being the pharmacy's designated payee, either as a registered third-party support entity if CMS and the facilitator allow it, or through a deposit account under a control agreement. That puts cash upstream of the wholesaler's weekly debit. Fallback is use-of-proceeds control, where the advance pays the MFP-drug invoice lines straight to the wholesaler. 3) Each week, score every MFP claim for dilution and buy the scored-eligible refunds at about 85% within two business days. The 15% reserve, net of our fee, is released when the actual MTF payment arrives. Recourse is limited to dilution through the reserve. There is no blanket credit recourse, and no 'non-recourse' promise we cannot keep. 4) Get the existing senior lender's consent or carve-out at onboarding, pitched as relief for their borrower's cash squeeze. Capital starts at $500k-$2M from a family office or regional bank, then a warehouse line from a specialty credit fund once 6 months of loss data exist.
why_now: The program has run since January 1, 2026 and the pain is measured and public (NCPA survey of 500+ owners, SCPC closure warnings). NCPA was still lobbying CMS on faster payment in September 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance, so no fix is in sight. On January 1, 2027 fifteen more drugs, including semaglutide, join and the float grows. The window is roughly the next three to four quarters, before a wholesaler or a bigger lender standardizes an answer.
revenue_model: Discount of about 0.9-1.25% per roughly 3-week cycle on purchased refunds (roughly 15-22% annualized), plus a $250 a month servicing fee per pharmacy. Illustrative unit economics for a pharmacy averaging $400k outstanding: $60-85k gross a year, about $36k cost of funds at 9%, under $6k expected dilution loss, leaving $20-35k contribution. Forty LTC pharmacies is about $16M outstanding and roughly $1M of annual contribution. An association endorsement, not Facebook groups, is affordable CAC at that revenue per account. Later, syndicate or sell seasoned receivables to a credit fund and keep servicing.
non_obvious_insight: LTC is the one segment where the parent's economics and its main risk both improve. Float per logo is 5-30x larger, so one association relationship replaces thousands of low-value retail leads. The dilution mode that worries everyone in retail, 340B lesser-of rejections, should be structurally small because nursing-home residents are rarely patients of 340B covered entities (verify pharmacy by pharmacy). The remaining dilution modes, discharge or death reversals and partial-cycle credits, are predictable from census and cycle-fill data that we ingest and a bank never sees. The lasting asset is a labeled dataset that maps each claim to its refund outcome. Interest is only how it is monetized.
first_30_days: Ask the Senior Care Pharmacy Coalition for introductions to 20 LTC owners and run willingness-to-pay interviews, pricing against 8-12% bank A/R lines and 30%+ MCAs. Sign 5 pharmacies to a free 60-day dilution audit in exchange for claims and remittance files. Build the dilution model in a notebook from those files. Ask the MTF help desk and a healthcare payments attorney what payee-designation options exist. Have a fintech attorney set the true-sale purchase structure, UCC filings and state commercial-financing disclosures. Line up a $500k credit line from a family office or regional bank. Fund the first three advances at $25-50k each with a 25% holdback.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: We do not sell reconciliation. SpendMend, Plenful, ScriptPro, Liberty and the free Beacon dashboards all compete on the report. Here the report is an internal underwriting input given away inside the advance, so there is no head-to-head feature race. Plenful targets health systems. Generic pharmacy lenders and Corporate Capital Direct advance against PBM A/R or MCA-style revenue and do not underwrite MFP refunds claim by claim. Live Oak's cheap SBA-style paper funds acquisitions, not a weekly refund float. We complement the senior lender through an intercreditor consent. The wholesaler's payment path, which the parent's research flagged as make-or-break, is handled by payee routing or direct invoice-line payment. That protects the wholesaler's payment, so it has no reason to object. Narrowing to LTC also sidesteps the small-float, high-CAC retail independent.

title: Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense
one_liner: A 48-hour, coder-certified benchmark report that tells defense lawyers and auto carriers what a letter-of-protection medical bill is actually worth.
customer: Insurance defense law firms and auto-carrier litigation/SIU units handling bodily-injury claims in tort-reform states (Florida, Georgia, Texas, Louisiana first). Volume firms pay per report. Carriers pay monthly.
problem: Plaintiff-side injury cases increasingly rest on treatment provided under letters of protection (LOP), where the provider is paid from the settlement and bills at a private rate card. Defense lawyers have to show what the care is really worth. Today that means a $3-5k billing expert, a slow turnaround, and a fight over methodology. Most claims examiners cannot read a CMS-1500 or UB-04, so inflated bills mostly get paid or settled at face value.
solution: Intake the itemized bill and records. Map every line to CPT/HCPCS and revenue codes and flag unbundling (e.g. 99215-25 plus separate injection administration, physician-owned ASC facility fees stacked on the professional fee, stacked imaging reads). Benchmark each line against Medicare multiples, hospital-posted commercial negotiated rates from price-transparency files, and local percentiles. The output is a Daubert-hardened PDF signed by a certified coder (CPC/CCS) with an optional expert declaration or testimony upsell. It is a methodology plus a template, so the marginal cost per report is about an hour of coder time.
why_now: Florida's 2023 tort reform made LOP arrangements discoverable and admitted evidence of amounts actually paid. Georgia's 2025 tort reform pushed similar rules, and other states are copying. Hospital price-transparency rules that took full effect in 2026 now require actual payment amounts where rates are percentages or algorithms, so a defensible local benchmark exists for the first time.
revenue_model: $295-$695 per report. Expert declaration or testimony at $1,500-$3,500. $2-5k/month subscriptions for carriers and volume firms with a report quota. Gross margin is high because coders are paid per report as contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Inside a hospital, chargemaster prices are understood to be fiction, and every biller knows what things really get paid. Injury lawyers have been arguing about 'reasonable value' without that insider map. Certified coders also know the tells of bills built for litigation rather than payment: modifier-25 patterns, unbundled facility fees, and E/M levels that no insurer would ever pay. The market is starved of people credentialed and willing to say so on paper. The moat is a coder bench plus a methodology that survives cross-examination, not software.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 CPC/CCS coders (ex-hospital, remote, contractors) and one defense-attorney advisor to review the methodology memo. Build the report template from the free Medicare fee schedules plus a few metro-area price-transparency files. Cold-email about 100 Florida and Georgia defense firms and claims managers, and offer 5 free reports on live cases in exchange for a methodology review and a testimonial. Convert the first 3-5 to $349 per report, then price the expert declaration as an add-on.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions, FAIR Health, EvenUp, Turquoise Health. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files.

title: Contractor-First Road Billing, Then Repair Lending
one_liner: Invert the parent: sell to plow and gravel contractors who each serve dozens of handshake roads with a get-paid rail that binds every household to its share, then use the payment history and recorded covenants to become the lender for culvert and washout repairs no bank will touch.
customer: Wedge: independent plow, gravel and excavation contractors serving 15-80 private roads and shared driveways each, starting in one snow-belt county in Maine or NH. Later payers: road associations as borrowers, and community banks, credit unions and CDFIs as capital partners who buy participations in the loans we originate and service.
problem: A contractor plows a 12-home road on a verbal 'we'll split it'. He bills one neighbor, who fronts the money and chases the others. After one or two free-riders the fronting neighbor quits, so the contractor drops the road or absorbs the loss. Contractors also front fuel, labor and equipment for a season and are paid unevenly. When a culvert or bridge fails, a $30-150k repair has no borrower, since there is no entity, no assets and no financials. NC's post-Helene program (verified) demanded a 50% cost share, a single point of contact and proof of ownership, so roads that could not front cash and had no organization were shut out. Both sides of the road are cash-starved for the same reason, which is no legal counterparty.
solution: Phase 1, sold this October to be live by first snow. RoadPay for contractors: the contractor enters a road's seasonal price. Each household receives an e-sign Road Service Agreement (pro-rata formula, driveway-level opt-in, dispute rule) with autopay via Stripe Connect direct charges, so we never hold funds. The contractor gets one dashboard across all roads, automatic reminders and statements, and monthly payouts. Phase 2, winter: Season Advance. We advance 60-80% of a signed road's seasonal contract to the contractor, funded by a small credit line, and repay ourselves from the households' autopay through April. We underwrite at the road level using percent of households on autopay, contractor history and driveway geometry. Phase 3, year 2: Graduation. Roads with two clean seasons are invited to record an assessment-lien covenant (through the closing-rescue-style formation service), because it lowers their borrowing rate. Phase 4: Repair and cost-share bridge loans. $25-150k loans to the association for culverts, regrading and bridge repairs, repaid over 5-10 years from assessments, funded by CDFI and community-bank participation with us as originator and servicer. The same facility can bridge the up-front 50% of state reimbursement programs.
why_now: Winter 2026-27 seasonal contracts get signed in October and November, about six weeks from today. That gives a hard deadline and a full season of data inside a six-month window. Embedded payments are now a commodity (Stripe Connect handles onboarding, split payouts and money-movement compliance), which is the Wardley shift that makes a two-person team viable. Post-Helene aid design (verified) teaches that organized counterparties get capital and unorganized roads do not. Document extraction makes reading recorded covenants cheap enough to underwrite each road. Contractor cost inflation since 2021 plausibly makes non-payment more painful (hypothesis to test in interviews).
revenue_model: Phase 1: 4% of billings collected, paid by the contractor (no per-household fee, so the PayHOA $2 anchor never applies). Phase 2: 3-5% fee on advances, turned several times per season. Phase 4: 2-3% origination plus about 1.5% servicing on loans sold to bank partners, plus net interest on any retained slice. Illustration: 100 contractors x 40 roads x $3,000 is about $12M of billings, so about $480k of rail revenue. If 5% of roads borrow $60k a year, that is about $12M of loans and roughly $300-500k of origination and servicing. Early revenue is small. The business becomes large only if the payment history and lien-backed collateral become the standard underwriting file for private roads, which is the 10x claim.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the best data and the strongest incentive is the contractor, not the neighbors. He knows every road's parcels, who pays, and which culvert is about to fail, and one phone call reaches 40 roads. His invoice is a high-frequency touchpoint neighbors already accept, whereas a formation package is a rare, compliance-flavored purchase. The legal entity stops being a product and becomes collateral. Neighbors will sign a recorded covenant to cut their repair loan rate from, say, 14% to 8%, which they would never do for 'compliance'. It also removes the parent's conflict of interest, since the contractor is the customer rather than a party we take a procurement fee from.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 plow and gravel contractors in one county through local snow-removal and excavation groups, feed and hardware stores and Facebook groups, and offer free first-season setup on their 3 most annoying roads. Have an attorney spend $2-4k reviewing a generic Road Service Agreement and consumer-ACH disclosures. Build a no-code MVP in 2 weeks (contractor form, e-sign page, Stripe Connect autopay, manual reconciliation sheet). Convert at least 25 roads before first snow and measure the household sign rate (target 75% or better), autopay success and contractor willingness to pay 4%. Open a conversation with one CDFI or community credit union about a $250k participation for advances. Riskiest assumptions: whether households sign a contractor-issued agreement, and how to handle free-riders on a shared road, since the contractor can skip non-signers' driveways but not the common road. Also confirm lending and money-transmission licensing with counsel before Phase 2.
lineage: mutation of I0048 ('Private Road Associations in a Box'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:
- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
